applies_why: The text decides a link collision (D6 vs C1) by holding the two sides' whole chains against each other, which is exactly the chain-versus-chain collision this rule governs.
quote: the challenger's seed/loins chain is footed but does not name Joseph as the begetter
rule_words: that no one of them states the contrary in its own words is the stating-verse test DG-61 retires, at a judge's seat as at a debater's, for either side
room: The phrase 'is footed but does not name Joseph as the begetter': on one reading the judge counts the chain's failure to state the Joseph-begetting link in so many words against it, the retired stating test; on the other, the judge merely notes the chain's footing never reaches the Joseph-paternity step. I chose the first reading because footing is already affirmed, so the 'but' clause adds a naming-based deficiency set parallel to the defender's, and it is what holds the footed challenger chain back from carrying the collision.
why: Having found the challenger's chain footed, the judge still weighed it down because it 'does not name Joseph as the begetter', applying the stating-verse test K-C retires for either side in a collision that must be weighed by footing alone.
